`mia` implements tools for microbiome analysis based on the
`SummarizedExperiment` [@SE], `SingleCellExperiment` [@SCE] and
`TreeSummarizedExperiment` [@TSE] infrastructure. Data wrangling and analysis
are the main scope of this package.

# Installation

To install `mia`, install `BiocManager` first, if it is not installed.
Afterwards use the `install` function from `BiocManager`.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("mia")
```

# Load *mia*

```{r load-packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library("mia")
```

# Overview of mia functions

The table below lists the functions of `mia` by use case. Most analysis
functions come in pairs: `get*()` returns the result, and `add*()` stores it
in the object, e.g. in `colData`, `rowData`, `reducedDim` or `metadata`.
Each function has a help page with examples, and the
[Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis](https://microbiome.github.io/OMA/) (OMA)
book shows them in complete workflows. Functions that are being
removed are listed in `?mia::deprecate`.

## Data import, export and conversion

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `importBIOM()`, `importQIIME2()`, `importQZA()`, `importMothur()`, `importMetaPhlAn()`, `importHUMAnN()`, `importTaxpasta()` | Import results of common pipelines as a `TreeSummarizedExperiment` (TreeSE) |
| `convertFromPhyloseq()`, `convertFromBIOM()`, `convertFromDADA2()` | Convert phyloseq, BIOM and DADA2 objects to TreeSE |
| `convertToPhyloseq()`, `convertToBIOM()` | Convert TreeSE to phyloseq or BIOM |
| `convertToMAE()`, `convertToTreeSE()` | Convert a TreeSE with alternative experiments to a `MultiAssayExperiment` and back |
| `exportQIIME2()`, `exportMothur()`, `exportRaw()` | Write data to files for QIIME 2, Mothur or as plain tables |
| `meltSE()` | Convert assay and metadata into a long (tidy) `data.frame` |
| `mergeSEs()` | Merge several objects into one |

## Data wrangling

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `subsetBy()` | Subset features or samples by conditions on the data, optionally collapsing the rest into "Other" |
| `agglomerateByRank()`, `agglomerateByRanks()` | Sum features to a taxonomic rank, or to all ranks as alternative experiments |
| `agglomerateByVariable()` | Sum features or samples by a grouping variable |
| `agglomerateBySet()`, `applyBySet()` | Summarise or apply a function by feature or sample sets |
| `splitOn()`, `unsplitOn()` | Split an object by a grouping variable and combine it back |
| `splitByRanks()`, `unsplitByRanks()` | Split by taxonomic ranks and combine back |
| `getReducedDimAttribute()` | Get attributes, e.g. explained variance, of an ordination |

## Taxonomy and trees

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `taxonomyRanks()`, `getTaxonomyRanks()`, `setTaxonomyRanks()` | Get or set the taxonomic ranks that mia recognises |
| `taxonomyRankEmpty()`, `checkTaxonomy()` | Check the taxonomy table |
| `getTaxonomyLabels()` | Create feature labels from the taxonomy |
| `mapTaxonomy()` | Look up taxa and their higher ranks |
| `getHierarchyTree()`, `addHierarchyTree()` | Create a tree from the taxonomy |
| `IdTaxaToDataFrame()` | Convert `DECIPHER::IdTaxa()` results to a taxonomy table |
| `parseTaxonomy()` | Split taxonomy strings such as `"k__Bacteria; p__Firmicutes"` into ranks |

## Transformation and normalisation

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `transformAssay()` | Relative abundance, CLR, rCLR, log, Hellinger, PA, z-score and other transformations |
| `rarefyAssay()` | Subsample counts to an equal library size |

## Quality control, summaries and core features

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `summary()` | Summary statistics of samples and features |
| `getQC()`, `addQC()` | Quality control metrics per sample and feature |
| `isContaminant()`, `isNotContaminant()`, `addContaminantQC()`, `addNotContaminantQC()` | Identify contaminants with the decontam package |
| `getPrevalence()`, `addPrevalence()` | Prevalence of each feature |
| `getPrevalent()`, `getRare()`, `getPrevalentAbundance()`, `addPrevalentAbundance()` | Prevalent and rare features, and the total abundance of prevalent features per sample |
| `getTop()`, `getUnique()` | Most abundant features, and the unique taxa of a rank |
| `getDominant()`, `addDominant()`, `summarizeDominance()` | The dominant feature of each sample |
| `getAbundant()`, `getLowAbundant()`, `getConditionallyLowAbundant()`, `getPermanentlyLowAbundant()`, `getAbundanceClass()`, `addAbundanceClass()` | Classify features as abundant or rare |

## Alpha diversity and other sample-wise indices

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `getAlpha()`, `addAlpha()` | Diversity, richness, evenness, dominance and rarity indices |
| `getDivergence()`, `addDivergence()` | Divergence of samples from a reference |
| `getDysbiosis()`, `addDysbiosis()` | Dysbiosis scores |

## Beta diversity and ordination

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `getDissimilarity()`, `addDissimilarity()` | Dissimilarities, e.g. Bray-Curtis, Aitchison, UniFrac, JSD and overlap |
| `getMDS()`, `addMDS()` | Multi-dimensional scaling (PCoA) |
| `getNMDS()`, `addNMDS()`, `calculateNMDS()`, `runNMDS()` | Non-metric MDS |
| `getPCA()`, `addPCA()` | Principal component analysis |
| `getRPCA()`, `addRPCA()` | Robust PCA |
| `getDPCoA()`, `addDPCoA()`, `calculateDPCoA()`, `runDPCoA()` | Double principal coordinate analysis |
| `getCCA()`, `addCCA()`, `getRDA()`, `addRDA()`, `calculateCCA()`, `runCCA()`, `calculateRDA()`, `runRDA()` | Constrained ordination (CCA, RDA and db-RDA) |
| `getNMF()`, `addNMF()`, `getLDA()`, `addLDA()` | Non-negative matrix factorisation and latent Dirichlet allocation |

## Clustering

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `getCluster()`, `addCluster()` | Cluster samples or features with any `bluster` method, including Dirichlet-multinomial mixtures |
| `calculateDMNgroup()`, `performDMNgroupCV()` | Dirichlet-multinomial mixture classification |

## Association and group comparison

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `getPERMANOVA()`, `addPERMANOVA()` | PERMANOVA with a test for homogeneity of dispersion |
| `getCrossAssociation()` | Correlations or other associations between two assays or experiments |
| `getMediation()`, `addMediation()` | Mediation analysis with features, assays or ordination components as mediators |

## Multi-omics

| Functions | Purpose |
|:---|:---|
| `getJointRPCA()`, `addJointRPCA()` | Joint robust PCA of several experiments |
| `getCrossAssociation()`, `convertToMAE()`, `mergeSEs()` | Associations and data integration across experiments |

## Example datasets

`GlobalPatterns`, `enterotype`, `esophagus`, `peerj13075`, `Tengeler2020`,
`HintikkaXOData`, `Tito2024QMP`, `ibdmdb` and `dmn_se` can be loaded with
`data()`, e.g. `data(GlobalPatterns, package = "mia")`. See
`?mia::"mia-datasets"`. Larger datasets are available in the
`microbiomeDataSets` package.

# Loading a `TreeSummarizedExperiment` object

A few example datasets are available via `mia`. For this vignette the 
`GlobalPatterns` dataset is loaded first.

```{r}
data(GlobalPatterns, package = "mia")
tse <- GlobalPatterns
tse
```

# Functions for working with microbiome data

One of the main topics for analysing microbiome data is the application of
taxonomic data to describe features measured. The interest lies in the 
connection between individual bacterial species and their relation to each 
other. 

`mia` does not rely on a specific object type to hold taxonomic data, but
uses specific columns in the `rowData` of a `TreeSummarizedExperiment` object.
`taxonomyRanks` can be used to construct a `character` vector of available 
taxonomic levels. This can be used, for example, for subsetting.

```{r}
# print the available taxonomic ranks
colnames(rowData(tse))
taxonomyRanks(tse)
# subset to taxonomic data only
rowData(tse)[,taxonomyRanks(tse)]
```

The columns are recognized case insensitive. Additional functions are 
available to check for validity of taxonomic information or generate labels
based on the taxonomic information.

```{r}
table(taxonomyRankEmpty(tse, "Species"))
head(getTaxonomyLabels(tse))
```

For more details see the man page `?taxonomyRanks`.

## Merging and agglomeration based on taxonomic information.

Agglomeration of data based on these taxonomic descriptors can be performed
using functions implemented in `mia`. In addition to the `aggValue` functions
provide by `TreeSummarizedExperiment` `agglomerateByRank` is available.
`agglomerateByRank` does not require tree data to be present.

`agglomerateByRank` constructs a `factor` to guide merging from the available
taxonomic information. For more information on merging have a look at the man
page via `?agglomerateByRank`.

```{r}
# agglomerate at the Family taxonomic rank
x1 <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "Family")
## How many taxa before/after agglomeration?
nrow(tse)
nrow(x1)
```

By default, the tree is removed, as it does not match the agglomerated data.

```{r}
rowTree(x1)
```

The tree can also be agglomerated alongside the data with
`update.tree = TRUE`. Each group is collapsed into the most recent common
ancestor of its features. This requires that groups are monophyletic, i.e.,
each group forms its own subtree. Otherwise, the tree is removed with a
warning. Here, the tree is agglomerated at the Kingdom rank.

```{r}
x2 <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "Kingdom", update.tree = TRUE)
rowTree(x2)
```

For `agglomerateByRank` to work, taxonomic data must be present. Even though
only one rank is available for the `enterotype` dataset, agglomeration can be
performed effectively de-duplicating entries for the genus level.

```{r}
data(enterotype, package = "mia")
taxonomyRanks(enterotype)
agglomerateByRank(enterotype)
```

To keep data tidy, the agglomerated data can be stored as an alternative 
experiment in the object of origin. With this synchronized sample subsetting
becomes very easy.

```{r}
altExp(tse, "family") <- x2
```

Keep in mind, that if you set `empty.rm = TRUE`, rows with `NA` or similar value
(defined via the `empty.fields` argument) will be removed. Depending on these
settings different number of rows will be returned.

```{r}
x1 <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "Species", empty.rm = TRUE)
altExp(tse,"species") <- agglomerateByRank(
    tse, rank = "Species", empty.rm = FALSE)
dim(x1)
dim(altExp(tse,"species"))
```

For convenience the function `agglomerateByRanks` is available, which
agglomerates data on all `ranks` selected. By default all available ranks will
be used. The output is compatible to be stored as alternative experiments.

```{r}
tse <- agglomerateByRanks(tse)
tse
altExpNames(tse)
```

## Constructing a tree from taxonomic data

Constructing a taxonomic tree from taxonomic data stored in `rowData` is quite
straightforward and uses mostly functions implemented in 
`TreeSummarizedExperiment`.

```{r}
taxa <- rowData(altExp(tse,"Species"))[,taxonomyRanks(tse)]
taxa_res <- resolveLoop(as.data.frame(taxa))
taxa_tree <- toTree(data = taxa_res)
taxa_tree$tip.label <- getTaxonomyLabels(altExp(tse,"Species"))
rowNodeLab <- getTaxonomyLabels(altExp(tse,"Species"), make.unique = FALSE)
altExp(tse,"Species") <- changeTree(
    altExp(tse,"Species"),
    rowTree = taxa_tree,
    rowNodeLab = rowNodeLab)
```

## Transformation of assay data

Transformation of count data stored in `assays` is also a main task when work
with microbiome data. `transformAssay` can be used for this and offers a few
choices of available transformations. A modified object is returned and the
transformed counts are stored in a new `assay`.

```{r}
assayNames(enterotype)
enterotype <- transformAssay(enterotype, method = "log10", pseudocount = 1)
assayNames(enterotype)
```

For more details have a look at the man page `?transformAssay`.  

Sub-sampling to equal number of counts per sample. Also known as rarefying.  
```{r}
data(GlobalPatterns, package = "mia")

tse.subsampled <- rarefyAssay(
    GlobalPatterns, 
    sample = 60000, 
    name = "subsampled",
    replace = TRUE,
    seed = 1938)
tse.subsampled

```

Alternatively, one can save both original TreeSE and subsampled TreeSE within a
MultiAssayExperiment object.  

```{r}
library(MultiAssayExperiment)
mae <- MultiAssayExperiment(
    c("originalTreeSE" = GlobalPatterns,
    "subsampledTreeSE" = tse.subsampled))
mae
```

```{r}
# To extract specifically the subsampled TreeSE
experiments(mae)$subsampledTreeSE
```

## Community indices

In the field of microbiome ecology several indices to describe samples and
community of samples are available. In this vignette we just want to give a
very brief introduction.

Functions for calculating alpha and beta diversity indices are available.
Using `addAlpha` multiple diversity indices are calculated by default
and results are stored automatically in `colData`. Selected indices can be 
calculated individually by setting `index = "shannon"` for example. 

```{r}
tse <- addAlpha(tse, index = "shannon")
colnames(colData(tse))[8:ncol(colData(tse))]
```

Beta diversity indices are used to describe inter-sample connections. 
Technically they are calculated as `dist` object and reduced dimensions can
be extracted using `cmdscale`. This is wrapped up in the `runMDS` function
of the `scater` package, but can be easily used to calculated beta diversity
indices using the established functions from the `vegan` package or any other
package using comparable inputs.

```{r}
library(scater)
altExp(tse,"Genus") <- runMDS(
    altExp(tse,"Genus"), 
    FUN = getDissimilarity,
    method = "bray",
    name = "BrayCurtis", 
    ncomponents = 5, 
    assay.type = "counts", 
    keep_dist = TRUE)
```

`getDissimilarity()` also calculates, e.g., JSD (`method = "jsd"`) and
UniFrac (`method = "unifrac"`, which uses the `rowTree`). `addMDS()` combines
both steps, and `addNMDS()`, `addPCA()`, `addRDA()` and `addDPCoA()` provide
other ordination methods. For more details see `?getDissimilarity` and
`?addMDS`.

```{r}
tse_phylum <- agglomerateByRank(GlobalPatterns, rank = "Phylum")
tse_phylum <- transformAssay(tse_phylum, method = "relabundance")
tse_phylum <- addMDS(
    tse_phylum, assay.type = "relabundance", method = "bray", name = "MDS_bray")
head(reducedDim(tse_phylum, "MDS_bray")[, 1:2])
```

`getPERMANOVA()` tests whether a variable explains differences in community
composition, and checks the homogeneity of dispersion between the groups.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
res <- getPERMANOVA(
    tse_phylum, assay.type = "relabundance", method = "bray",
    formula = x ~ SampleType, permutations = 99)
res$permanova
```

## Other indices

`addAlpha()` also calculates indices of richness, evenness, dominance and
rarity. Each index is stored in its own `colData` column.

```{r}
tse_phylum <- addAlpha(
    tse_phylum, assay.type = "counts",
    index = c("observed_richness", "pielou", "gini_dominance"))
head(colData(tse_phylum)[, c("observed_richness", "pielou", "gini_dominance")])
```

## Clustering

`addCluster()` clusters samples or features with methods from the `bluster`
package and stores the clusters in `colData` or `rowData`.

```{r}
library(bluster)
tse_phylum <- addCluster(
    tse_phylum, assay.type = "relabundance", by = "samples",
    BLUSPARAM = HclustParam(
        metric = "bray", dist.fun = vegan::vegdist, cut.dynamic = FALSE,
        cut.params = list(k = 3)))
table(tse_phylum$cluster, tse_phylum$SampleType)
```

# Utility functions

To make migration and adoption as easy as possible several utility functions
are available.

## Data loading functions

Functions to load data from `biom` files, `QIIME2` output, `DADA2` objects 
[@dada2] or `phyloseq` objects are available. 

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(phyloseq)
data(esophagus, package = "phyloseq")
```

```{r}
esophagus
esophagus <- convertFromPhyloseq(esophagus)
esophagus
```

For more details have a look at the man page, for examples 
`?convert`.

## General wrapper functions 

Row-wise or column-wise assay data subsetting.

```{r}
# Specific taxa
assay(tse['522457',], "counts") |> head()
# Specific sample
assay(tse[,'CC1'], "counts") |> head()

```

`subsetBy()` subsets features or samples by conditions on the data. With
`collapse = TRUE`, the features that are left out are summed into one
feature called "Other".

```{r}
tse_sub <- subsetBy(
    tse_phylum, rows = rowMeans(relabundance) > 0.01, collapse = TRUE)
rownames(tse_sub)
# Samples with at least 500,000 reads
dim(subsetBy(tse_phylum, cols = colSums(counts) >= 500000))
```

`summary()` gives summary statistics of the samples and features.

```{r}
summary(tse_phylum, assay.type = "counts")
```

## Selecting most interesting features 

`getTop` returns a vector of the most `top` abundant feature IDs.

```{r}
data(esophagus, package = "mia")
top_taxa <- getTop(
    esophagus,
    method = "mean",
    top = 5,
    assay.type = "counts")
top_taxa
```

`getPrevalent()` returns the features that exceed a detection limit in a given
fraction of the samples, and `addPrevalence()` stores the prevalence of each
feature in `rowData`.

```{r}
getPrevalent(
    tse_phylum, assay.type = "relabundance", detection = 0.01,
    prevalence = 0.5)
tse_phylum <- addPrevalence(
    tse_phylum, assay.type = "relabundance", detection = 0.01)
head(sort(rowData(tse_phylum)$prevalence, decreasing = TRUE))
```

`getDominant()` gives the most abundant feature of each sample.

```{r}
table(getDominant(tse_phylum, assay.type = "counts"))
```

## Generating tidy data

To generate tidy data as used and required in most of the tidyverse, 
`meltSE` can be used. A `data.frame` in the long format will be returned.

```{r}
molten_data <- meltSE(
    tse,
    assay.type = "counts",
    add.row = TRUE,
    add.col = TRUE
)
molten_data
```
